cards.front: What is Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for, in one sentence?
cards.back: Ingesting and holding a **real-time stream** of records (clicks, IoT telemetry, logs) so several consumers can process it within milliseconds and **replay** it later.

cards.front: What decides which shard a Kinesis record goes to?
cards.back: Its **partition key**: Kinesis hashes the key (MD5) and maps the result to a shard's hash key range. Same key, same shard.

cards.front: What ordering does Kinesis Data Streams guarantee?
cards.back: Order **per partition key (within a shard)**. There is no global order across shards.

cards.front: Write and read capacity of one provisioned Kinesis shard?
cards.back: **In**: 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s. **Out**: 2 MB/s (and 5 `GetRecords` calls/s), shared by all standard consumers.

cards.front: Default and maximum retention of a Kinesis data stream?
cards.back: **24 hours** by default, up to **365 days** (8,760 hours). Retention beyond 24 hours costs extra.

cards.front: Can you delete a specific record from a Kinesis data stream after a consumer reads it?
cards.back: **No.** Records are immutable and stay until the retention period expires. Reading does not remove them, which is what makes replay possible.

cards.front: Maximum record payload in Kinesis Data Streams today?
cards.back: **1 MiB by default**; a stream's maximum record size can be raised to **10 MiB**, intended for occasional large records. Shard throughput limits stay the same.
cards.updated: Configurable up to 10 MiB since October 2025; default remains 1 MiB.

cards.front: Provisioned vs on-demand capacity mode: when do you pick each?
cards.back: **Provisioned** for steady, forecastable traffic (you set shards, pay per shard-hour). **On-demand** for spiky or unknown traffic (auto-scales to double the 30-day peak, pay per GB, plus a per-stream-hour fee in On-demand Standard).

cards.front: What is Kinesis On-demand Advantage?
cards.back: An **account-level** on-demand setting: no per-stream fee, at least 60% cheaper per GB, optional warm throughput, up to 50 enhanced fan-out consumers, in exchange for a minimum 25 MiB/s ingest and retrieval commitment per Region.
cards.updated: New mode added after the slides were written.

cards.front: What does enhanced fan-out give a Kinesis consumer?
cards.back: Its **own 2 MB/s per shard**, delivered by **push** over HTTP/2 (`SubscribeToShard`) with about 70 ms latency, instead of sharing 2 MB/s per shard with other consumers.

cards.front: How many enhanced fan-out consumers can register on one stream?
cards.back: **20** per stream in On-demand Standard and Provisioned modes; **50** with On-demand Advantage.

cards.front: KPL vs KCL?
cards.back: **KPL** (Kinesis Producer Library) helps **producers** batch, aggregate and retry writes. **KCL** (Kinesis Client Library) helps **consumers** share shards across workers and checkpoint progress in DynamoDB.

cards.front: A producer gets `ProvisionedThroughputExceededException` on one shard while others are idle. Likely cause and fix?
cards.back: A **hot shard** from a low-cardinality partition key. Use a key with many distinct values (for example device ID), add retries/batching, and add shards or use on-demand if total volume is too high.

cards.front: How is data in a Kinesis data stream encrypted?
cards.back: **In transit** with HTTPS endpoints; **at rest** with server-side encryption using an AWS KMS key (AWS managed or customer managed). Client-side encryption is optional and self-managed.

cards.front: What is Amazon Data Firehose?
cards.back: A **fully managed, serverless** service (formerly Kinesis Data Firehose) that buffers streaming data and **delivers it in batches** to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch, partner tools or HTTP endpoints, with no consumer code.

cards.front: What triggers a Firehose delivery to the destination?
cards.back: Whichever comes first: the **buffer size** (for S3 1–128 MiB, default 5 MiB) or the **buffer interval** (0–900 s, default 300 s).
cards.updated: Interval can now go down to 0 seconds (zero buffering); it used to start at 60 seconds.

cards.front: Maximum size of a record sent to Amazon Data Firehose?
cards.back: **1,000 KiB** (before base64 encoding).

cards.front: How do you convert CSV records to Parquet with Firehose?
cards.back: Add a **Lambda transformation** that turns CSV into JSON, then enable **record format conversion** (JSON to Parquet or ORC) using a schema in the **AWS Glue Data Catalog**.

cards.front: How does Firehose deliver data into Amazon Redshift?
cards.back: It writes the batch to an **intermediate S3 bucket**, then runs a Redshift **`COPY`** command to load it.

cards.front: Can Firehose replay data or serve several independent consumers?
cards.back: **No.** Firehose stores nothing and has one destination per stream. For replay or many consumers, put **Kinesis Data Streams** in front.

cards.front: Kinesis Data Streams vs Firehose: latency words the exam uses?
cards.back: Kinesis Data Streams = **real-time** (about 70–200 ms). Firehose = **near real-time** (buffered for seconds to minutes).

cards.front: SQS vs SNS vs Kinesis in one line each?
cards.back: **SQS**: workers pull, message deleted after processing. **SNS**: push copies to many subscribers, nothing stored. **Kinesis**: ordered stream kept for days, many consumers, replayable.

cards.front: When is Amazon MQ the right answer?
cards.back: When an existing app uses **open broker protocols** (AMQP, MQTT, STOMP, OpenWire, WebSocket, JMS) with ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ and you want to move it to AWS **without rewriting** it for SQS/SNS.

cards.front: Which engines does Amazon MQ manage?
cards.back: **Apache ActiveMQ Classic** and **RabbitMQ**. Both offer queues (like SQS) and topics or exchanges for pub/sub (like SNS).

cards.front: How does Amazon MQ for ActiveMQ achieve high availability?
cards.back: An **active/standby** pair of brokers in **two AZs** sharing **Amazon EFS** storage; clients use a failover URL listing both endpoints and reconnect to the standby when it takes over.

cards.front: How does Amazon MQ for RabbitMQ achieve high availability?
cards.back: A **cluster deployment** of **three broker nodes** across AZs behind a Network Load Balancer, with data replicated between nodes (quorum queues are the default on RabbitMQ 4).
cards.updated: RabbitMQ 4.2/4.3 on mq.m7g make quorum queues the default queue type.

cards.front: Why does Amazon MQ not scale like SQS or SNS?
cards.back: It runs on **broker instances** you size and pay for per hour, so capacity is bounded by the instance type; SQS and SNS are serverless and scale almost without limit.

cards.front: Since August 2026, how can an on-demand Kinesis data stream land data in S3 without Firehose?
cards.back: With built-in **data delivery**: directly to a general purpose S3 bucket (raw format) or to Apache Iceberg **streaming tables** on S3 Tables, with 5–15 minute freshness and no consumer code.
cards.updated: Feature launched in August 2026, after the slides.

cards.front: Starting write capacity of a new on-demand Kinesis data stream?
cards.back: **4 MB/s or 4,000 records/s** of writes (8 MB/s of reads). It then scales automatically to absorb up to **double the peak** seen in the previous 30 days.

cards.front: An answer offers "Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL" for real-time stream analytics. What is the current service?
cards.back: **Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink** (SQL, Java, Python, Scala). Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL took no new apps from 15 October 2025 and existing apps were deleted from 27 January 2026.
cards.updated: Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL was discontinued after the slides were written.
